movement_source: row 'Total loan impairment expense', column Full Year Ended 30 Jun 25 $M -> column Full Year Ended 30 Jun 26 $M
headline: CBA's loan impairment expense rose to $788m in FY26 from $726m in FY25, an increase of $62m or 9% (the slide pack prints the same movement as 8.5%). The loss rate rose 1bp to 8bps of average gross loans and acceptances, with corporate improving 14→12bps and consumer 5→6bps. The whole increase is a collective-provision story: net collective provision funding rose $150m to $606m on portfolio growth, increased geopolitical risk and macroeconomic uncertainty, with the Downside scenario weighting increased during the year. Individually assessed provisioning went the other way — new and increased IAP fell $17m to $422m and write-backs rose $71m to $240m, an $88m offset. By division, Retail +$106m to $378m and New Zealand +$11m to $66m drove the rise, partly offset by Business Banking -$45m to $310m and Institutional -$16m to $33m. Total provision stock rose only $99m to $6,476m.

drivers.columns: Full Year Ended 30 Jun 26 vs 30 Jun 25 $M
drivers.narrative: Net collective provision funding rose to $606m from $456m. The bank attributes the higher charge to "portfolio growth and increased global macroeconomic uncertainty". Retail Banking Services +$106m to $378m on "increased geopolitical risk, macroeconomic uncertainty, and rising cost-of-living pressures"; New Zealand +$11m to $66m on "deterioration in the unemployment outlook". Home loan 90+ arrears 0.69%→0.75%.

drivers.columns: Full Year Ended 30 Jun 26 vs 30 Jun 25 $M
drivers.narrative: Portfolio growth is named inside the $150m collective bar, not separately quantified. Business Banking and Institutional both cite "higher collective provisions reflecting portfolio growth". Corporate collective provision stock +$172m or 7% to $2,797m on portfolio growth; Retail home loan growth $41.4bn or 8%, above system. Stock movements are context, not the charge.

drivers.columns: Full Year Ended 30 Jun 26 vs 30 Jun 25 $M
drivers.narrative: Not separately quantified in the charge. "the weighting to the Downside scenario has been increased during the year with a commensurate decrease in the Central scenario" — an upward force. Partly offset: consumer collective provisions fell $48m to $2,888m on "rising house prices" and "more targeted forward-looking adjustments for higher risk customer cohorts", a balance-sheet movement only.

drivers.columns: Full Year Ended 30 Jun 26 vs 30 Jun 25 $M
drivers.narrative: New and increased individually assessed provisioning fell to $422m from $439m. Business Banking -$45m to $310m on "lower individually assessed provision charges"; Institutional -$16m to $33m on "release of individually assessed provisions"; New Zealand cites "lower individually assessed provisions and lower consumer finance write-offs" within its +$11m. Corporate IAP stock -$6m to $694m.

drivers.columns: Full Year Ended 30 Jun 26 vs 30 Jun 25 $M
drivers.narrative: Write-backs of individually assessed provisions grew to $240m from $169m, a larger credit to the charge. Business Banking's -$45m is driven by "lower individually assessed provision charges, including an increase in write-backs"; corporate IAP stock fell $6m to $694m "driven by write-backs and write-offs". Separately, collective impairment losses recovered rose to $160m from $130m.

notable_items: Loan impairment expense is presented on a continuing operations basis in both years; FY25 comparatives 'have been restated to conform to presentation in the current period'.
Restructuring and notable items of $170m in FY26 relate to legal-proceeding provisions in NZ, an ASIC Better Banking goodwill payment and customer remediation — none sit in the impairment line.

disagreements.topic: FY26 vs FY25 LIE growth rate
disagreements.explanation: Both rest on the same $726m→$788m levels ($62m, 8.54%). The results book rounds to a whole percent; the slide prints one decimal. No substantive difference.

The FY26 profit announcement footnotes that 'Comparative information has been restated to conform to presentation in the current period.' Restated comparatives from the newer document win, and the FY26 book's own bullets ($106m Retail, -$45m Business) are computed off them. Group total $726m is unchanged.

limitations: CBA publishes no waterfall/bridge chart for the FY26 vs FY25 impairment charge. The quantified bridge is built by subtracting the two full-year columns of the provision-type rows in note 2.2 (p118), so the arithmetic is mine, not the bank's framing — hence confidence capped below chart level. The three components (+150, -17, -71) sum exactly to the stated +$62m, leaving zero residual.

The bank does not quantify how much of the $150m collective bar is portfolio growth versus risk migration versus FLA/MES changes; collective.volume and overlays_fla are therefore carried unquantified rather than assigned borrowed numbers.

Divisional deltas are the 'where', not a second bridge — they must not be added to the provision-type bridge. Note the FY26 divisional table's Corporate Centre and Other moved from a $5m benefit to a $1m expense.

Provision-stock movements quoted in the narratives (corporate collective +$172m to $2,797m, consumer collective -$48m to $2,888m, total provisions +$99m to $6,476m) are balance-sheet levels that also absorb write-offs and recoveries; they are context and are not the period's charge.

The consumer collective provision DECREASE of $48m sits beside a Retail charge INCREASE of $106m — the stock fell because write-offs ($618m) exceeded funding, so the stock direction must not be read as the charge direction.
Sectoral FLA commentary on presentation p71 is explicitly framed as 'last 6 months', a half-year span, so it annotates rather than explains the full-year movement.
